paragraphs.text: Recurrent hydatidiform mole-6 is a female reproductive disorder in which affected women have repeated molar pregnancies, often with miscarriages. Rezaei et al. (2024) reported biallelic deleterious variants in 6 genes, including KASH5, in patients with recurrent androgenetic hydatidiform moles. Five of these genes are essential for meiosis I, and deficiency of these genes leads to premature ovarian insufficiency. Saharan et al. (2026) reported that HYDM6 can progress to recurrent and metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN).

paragraphs.text: In the same study that reported KASH5 variants, Rezaei et al. (2024) also found biallelic variants in other meiosis or ovarian genes in patients with recurrent hydatidiform moles. In an Iranian proband (1802) born to consanguineous parents who were third-degree cousins, they used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous frameshift variant in the HFM1 gene, c.3124dupT (p.Tyr1042LeufsTer7). The variant lay in a 25-Mb run of homozygosity on chromosome 1. It was also homozygous in her affected sister, who had 3 hydatidiform moles, and heterozygous in both parents. The CHM from the affected sister was androgenetic monospermic. An affected maternal aunt had 1 mole at age 23 and was then unable to conceive. She was compound heterozygous for c.3124dupT and a predicted splice acceptor variant, c.1159-1G-A.

paragraphs.text: Rezaei et al. (2024) identified a homozygous MAJIN splice donor variant, c.349+1G-T, in an Italian patient (1824) born to consanguineous parents. She had 2 androgenetic monospermic, p57-negative CHMs followed by secondary infertility, and at age 25 her ovarian volumes were markedly reduced (1.1 and 2.5 cm3). Her heterozygous carrier mother had had 1 triploid dispermic partial mole and irregular menses. The authors suggested that monoallelic variants in MAJIN, and perhaps in other meiotic genes, may underlie milder phenotypes.

paragraphs.text: Rezaei et al. (2024) also identified a homozygous SYCP2 splice acceptor variant (c.2530-2A-G) in an Egyptian patient (1954) with 4 CHMs and primary and secondary infertility. In another Egyptian patient (2136), who had 6 early miscarriages, 3 failed ICSI cycles, 1 hydatidiform mole, and low anti-Mullerian hormone, they found a homozygous MEIOB nonsense variant (c.814C-T; R272X). In a South Asian patient (1690) with 5 CHMs, they found a homozygous FOXL2 missense variant, c.500T-C (F167S), which they classified as a variant of uncertain significance. The authors stated that this single variant did not allow conclusions about a causal role for FOXL2. Saharan et al. (2026) identified a heterozygous FOXL2 variant, G187D, in a woman with recurrent hydatidiform moles. This variant had previously been reported in patients with premature ovarian insufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Rezaei et al. (2024) screened 310 patients with reproductive loss for monoallelic loss-of-function variants in 494 ovarian and meiosis genes. They found 77 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in 55 genes in 68 patients (21.8%). BRCA2 and ZP3 variants were significantly enriched compared with gnomAD. Genes in the DNA metabolism protein class accounted for 11% of the input gene list (53 of 482) but 25% of genes with validated variants in patients (14 of 57) (P = 0.003). The authors concluded that such monoallelic variants most likely confer genetic susceptibility.

paragraphs.text: In a woman with recurrent hydatidiform moles, Saharan et al. (2026) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a very rare homozygous variant in KASH5, arg196-to-his (R196H), and confirmed it by Sanger sequencing. The patient had recurrent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and her sister, who also had recurrent moles, died of metastatic GTN. The authors concluded that their findings further supported an association of KASH5 variants with recurrent hydatidiform mole.

paragraphs.text: Rezaei et al. (2024) suggested that meiosis I defects affecting synapsis and recombination play a major role in the genesis of androgenetic complete moles. They also suggested that recurrent androgenetic complete moles may be a sign of accelerated ovarian aging or a mild form of premature ovarian insufficiency, which would explain why the risk rises with advanced maternal age.

paragraphs.text: In a woman with recurrent hydatidiform moles and recurrent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, Saharan et al. (2026) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a very rare homozygous arg196-to-his (R196H) variant in the KASH5 gene and confirmed it by Sanger sequencing. Her sister also had recurrent moles and died of metastatic GTN.
